clientId.description:
ClientID is the application the token was issued to, and the only identity
a client_credentials token carries — this provider leaves `sub` empty for
one. Absent for a token that names neither client_id nor azp.

email.description: Email is the caller's email when the token carried the claim.

subject.description: Subject is the identity provider's stable subject claim.

job.description:
Job is the Kubernetes Job doing the work, in the panel's own namespace. It
has a status and a log, which is what makes "did it work" a question with a
direct answer rather than one inferred by reading the release back.

message.description:
Message says how to find out what happened, because the record of what was
asked for and the record of what happened are two different systems.

operation.description:
Operation is rollout, rollback, or uninstall. Not install or upgrade:
which of those a rollout turns out to be is decided by the Job, from what
Helm has when the work starts.

appVersion.description:
AppVersion is what the chart says it packages, which is usually what an
operator actually recognises — a chart version of 6.9.1 means nothing next
to an app version of 1.29.0.

valuesYaml.description: ValuesYAML may be empty, which means the chart's own defaults.

chartRef.description:
ChartRef is the reference an operator typed, and the thing a new version
is fetched from. It never carries credentials.

ChartRef is the reference an operator typed, and the thing a new version
is fetched from. It never carries credentials.

releaseError.description:
ReleaseError says why the live release could not be read, when it could
not. Reported rather than swallowed: a page that silently shows a record
with no release beside it is a page that says "nothing is deployed" when
what happened was a refused Secret read.

state.description:
State is this record measured against the cluster — see the State
constants.

status.description: Status is Helm's own word for the live release, empty when there is none.

versions.description: Versions are every declared version, newest first.

ChartRef is the reference an operator typed, and the thing a new version
is fetched from. It never carries credentials.

State is this record measured against the cluster — see the State
constants.

status.description: Status is Helm's own word for the live release, empty when there is none.

helm.DeploymentVersion.description:
Current is the newest declared version, which is what a rollout would
apply.

helmRevision.description: HelmRevision lines this version up against Helm's own history.

rolledOutAt.description: RolledOutAt is nil until this version reached the cluster.

valuesYaml.description: ValuesYAML is the document as it was written, comments and all.

namespace.description:
Namespace and Release are what the operation targets, not where the Job
runs — the Job always runs in the panel's own namespace.

phase.description: Phase is pending, running, succeeded, or failed.

pod.description: Pod is empty until one has been scheduled, which is not immediate.

reason.description:
Reason says why, when a Job failed for a reason Kubernetes named —
DeadlineExceeded, BackoffLimitExceeded. Helm's own account of a failure is
in the log, not here.

description.description:
Description is the log entry Helm writes on each revision: "Upgrade
complete", or the reason one failed. It is the most useful field on a
broken release and the least interesting on a healthy one.

revision.description:
Revision counts up from 1 and never repeats, including across a rollback:
rolling back to revision 2 creates revision 5 rather than returning to 2.

status.description:
Status is Helm's own vocabulary — deployed, failed, pending-upgrade,
superseded, uninstalling — passed through rather than mapped, because an
operator reading it here and running `helm status` should see one word.

helm.ReleaseDetail.description:
Release is what Helm has, and nil when the release is not installed or
could not be read.

description.description:
Description is the log entry Helm writes on each revision: "Upgrade
complete", or the reason one failed. It is the most useful field on a
broken release and the least interesting on a healthy one.

notes.description:
Notes is the chart's rendered NOTES.txt, which is where a chart says how to
reach what it just installed.

revision.description:
Revision counts up from 1 and never repeats, including across a rollback:
rolling back to revision 2 creates revision 5 rather than returning to 2.

status.description:
Status is Helm's own vocabulary — deployed, failed, pending-upgrade,
superseded, uninstalling — passed through rather than mapped, because an
operator reading it here and running `helm status` should see one word.

values.description:
Values are the values supplied when the release was installed or upgraded,
and not the coalesced set. The coalesced set is the chart's entire
values.yaml merged with these, which an operator would then re-submit as
their own — pinning every default the chart ships with, forever.

revision.description:
Revision is required. Helm defaults a missing one to "the previous
revision", which is a different operation from the one an operator clicked
in a table of revisions, and defaulting to it would sometimes do the right
thing quietly and sometimes the wrong thing quietly.

rollbackOnFailure.description:
RollbackOnFailure is off by default, and this is the one default worth
arguing about. With it on, a failed rollout is undone and the release ends
up deployed on a *new* revision — so a pipeline polling for a terminal
status reads success for a deploy that did not deploy.

version.description:
Version is the declared version to apply, and zero means the newest. Naming
one is how "restore what we had on Tuesday" works without editing anything.

error.description: Error is a stable, machine-readable code.

message.description: Message is a human-readable explanation. It never carries internal detail.

ports.description:
Ports are rendered as "80→8080/TCP", which is the form that answers what
the caller connects to and what the container is listening on.

type.description: Type is ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, or ExternalName.

lastTransition.description:
LastTransition is when it last changed, which is what says whether a
failing condition is new or has been there all along.

kube.Filesystem.description:
Filesystem is the node's root disk. Nil unless node stats are switched on:
reading them needs a grant on the kubelet that the panel does not hold by
default. See charts/admin/templates/api/rbac.yaml.

labels.description:
Labels are carried because policy is decided from them — whether the
namespace is protected, and whether Helm may write to it — and because the
panel shows an operator why a namespace has no delete button.

protected.description:
Protected reports that this namespace may not be deleted, and why. Decided
by internal/nspolicy from the name and the labels above, not by the cluster.

pressure.description:
Pressure lists the conditions that are true right now and should not be —
MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure. Empty is the healthy case.

roles.description:
Roles come from the node-role.kubernetes.io/* labels, which is the only
place Kubernetes records them.

status.description:
Status is the summary an operator reads first: Ready, NotReady, or
Ready,SchedulingDisabled for a cordoned node, which the conditions alone do
not say.

pressure.description: Pressure counts nodes reporting any pressure condition.

containers.description:
Containers names each one, which a log request must do when there is more
than one. Init containers are included, last.

phase.description:
Phase is Kubernetes' own phase, and Status is the more useful summary —
"Terminating" or a waiting container's reason, which the phase does not say.

ready.description:
Ready counts containers, not pods: "1/2" is a running pod that is not
serving, which is the case worth seeing.

kube.Resources.description:
Usage is the sum over the nodes that reported one, and is meaningless
unless Summary.MetricsAvailable is true — a sum of nothing is zero, and
zero is also what a genuinely idle cluster reports. This is a plain value
rather than the pointer Node.Usage is because a total has one flag covering
it, where a per-node reading has to say which nodes were measured.

Even with MetricsAvailable true, a node that metrics-server has not sampled
yet contributes nothing, so this can understate a cluster that is still
warming up.

kube.Scale.description: Scale is absent for a DaemonSet, which has no replica count to set.

current.description: Current is how many exist right now, which lags Replicas during a rollout.

replicas.description: Replicas is the desired count — what the controller was told to run.

A pointer so absent can be told from zero. int32 would make `{}` decode to
0, and 0 is a legitimate replica count — so a request that named no count
at all would scale the workload down to nothing. Scaling to zero has to be
something the caller asked for.

capacityBytes.description:
CapacityBytes counts only bound claims. An unbound claim has no capacity
yet, and counting what it asked for would report space that does not exist.

unbound.description:
Unbound is every claim that is not Bound, which is Pending and Lost
together. They are counted as one because they mean the same thing to the
operator — a workload asked for storage and does not have it — and named
for what they have in common rather than for the more common of the two.

metricsAvailable.description:
MetricsAvailable reports whether metrics-server answered. When false the
usage figures are zero because nothing measured them, not because nothing
is running — a distinction the dashboard has to draw for the operator.

claim.description: Claim is the namespace/name this volume is bound to, empty when unbound.

reclaimPolicy.description:
ReclaimPolicy decides what happens to the data when the claim goes away,
which is the field worth seeing before deleting anything.

requestedBytes.description:
Requested is what the claim asked for and Capacity what it actually got.
A provisioner may round up, so the two disagreeing is normal rather than a
fault — but only Capacity says how much space there really is.

status.description:
Status is the claim's phase: Bound, Pending, or Lost. A Pending claim is
usually the reason a StatefulSet's pod will not start.

volumeName.description: VolumeName is the PersistentVolume bound to this claim, empty while pending.

desired.description:
Desired is how many replicas the controller wants, and Ready how many are
serving. A DaemonSet's desired count is per node rather than configured.

images.description:
Images are the container images the pod template runs, which is what says
which version is deployed.

conditions.description:
Conditions are the controller's own, which carry the reason a rollout is
stuck when the replica counts only show that it is.

events.description: Events are scoped to this workload and its pods, most recent first.

updated.description:
Replicas is what the controller reports beyond ready — updated and
available, which is how a rollout that has stalled is told from one that is
merely in progress.

degraded.description:
Degraded is the count with fewer ready replicas than desired, which is the
number that answers "is anything wrong" on its own.

collection.description: Collection is created inside the new database, bringing it into existence.

roles.description:
Roles granted to the user. Each names a role and the database it applies
to; an empty Database on a role means the database the user is created in.

empty.description: Empty is true for a database the server lists but which holds nothing.

sizeBytes.description: SizeBytes is the size on disk as the server reports it.

filter.description: Filter is a MongoDB query document. Empty matches everything.

limit.description: Limit caps the documents returned, up to the server-side maximum.

projection.description: Projection selects fields. Empty returns whole documents.

documents.description:
Documents are rendered as extended-JSON strings, one per document. The panel
displays them; carrying BSON's types faithfully through JSON would mean a
type map to keep current for no gain.

truncated.description:
Truncated reports that the result was cut at the limit, so the panel can say
so rather than presenting a partial answer as the whole one.

password.description:
Password, when set, replaces the existing one. Empty leaves it alone — a
password cannot be read back, so an edit form that omits it means "unchanged"
rather than "remove".

owner.description:
Owner is the role that will own it. Empty leaves it owned by the role the
panel connects as.

canCreateDatabase.description:
CanCreateDatabase and CanCreateRole grant the two privileges an application
role sometimes needs. Superuser is deliberately not offered.

canLogin.description:
CanLogin makes the role a user rather than a group. Defaults to false, so
creating a login role is a deliberate act.

password.description:
Password is required when CanLogin is true and must be empty otherwise —
a password on a role that cannot log in is refused rather than dropped, so
the caller is never left believing it set one. It never reaches the server
as plaintext; a SCRAM verifier is derived from it first.

encoding.description: Encoding is the character set, e.g. UTF8.

owner.description: Owner is the role that owns it.

sizeBytes.description:
SizeBytes is the on-disk size. Absent (0) when the connecting role cannot
read it, which is not an error worth failing a listing over.

sql.description:
SQL is a single read-only statement. It is not parsed or filtered here —
PostgreSQL enforces the read-only part itself. See Service.Query.

columns.description: Columns are in the order the statement selected them.

elapsedMs.description:
ElapsedMs is how long the server took, which is most of what a query is run
for when it is being tuned rather than read.

rows.description:
Rows hold values already rendered as strings. The panel displays them and
does not compute on them, and preserving every PostgreSQL type through JSON
would mean a type map that has to be kept current for no gain.

truncated.description:
Truncated reports that the result was cut at the row cap, so the panel can
say so rather than presenting a partial answer as the whole one.

canCreateDatabase.description:
CanCreateDatabase and CanCreateRole are the two privileges worth granting a
role that administers its own application.

canLogin.description: CanLogin distinguishes a user from a group.

connectionLimit.description: ConnectionLimit is -1 when unlimited, which is the default.

isSuperuser.description:
IsSuperuser is reported so the panel can show which roles bypass every
permission check. The panel never creates one.

connectionLimit.description: ConnectionLimit is -1 for unlimited, which is PostgreSQL's own default.

password.description:
Password, when set, replaces the existing one. Never sent as plaintext: a
SCRAM verifier is derived from it first, the same as on create.

BearerAuth.description: An OAuth 2.1 access token from the configured provider.

info.description:
Manages the home lab's PostgreSQL and MongoDB services, and reads its Kubernetes cluster.
Every /api endpoint needs a bearer access token from the configured OpenID Connect
provider. There are no API keys: a caller acts as the person who signed in, and an
agent carries that person's token.
info.title: home-lab Admin API

get.description:
The reference is an OCI or HTTPS chart URL whose last path segment is the
chart name — oci://ghcr.io/org/charts/podinfo, or
https://stefanprodan.github.io/podinfo/podinfo. The registry is contacted
when this is called, so an unreachable one is a 502 rather than an empty list.
get.summary: List the versions a chart reference offers

get.description:
Each carries the newest declared version and how it stands against the
cluster: in-sync, pending, drifted, not-installed, or unknown when the
live release could not be read.

post.description:
Writes the record and its first version. Nothing reaches the cluster until
a rollout, so a half-written values file is a saved draft rather than a
failed install.

oneOf.description: The chart, namespace and first values

requestBody.description: The chart, namespace and first values

delete.description:
Removes this lab's record and every version of it. The release on the
cluster is untouched — uninstalling it is a separate request.

put.description:
Takes a chart version and optional values overrides, merges the overrides
over the newest declared values, stores the result as a new version, and
rolls it out. Omitting values carries the previous ones forward unchanged,
comments included, so a pipeline that owns only a chart tag cannot erase an
operator's configuration.

Accepted, not performed. Poll the deployment until its status is no longer
pending, then assert BOTH that the status is deployed AND that the chart
version equals what was asked for: with rollbackOnFailure set, a failed
deploy is undone and lands "deployed" on the previous version.
put.summary: Deploy a new chart version from a pipeline

post.description:
Accepted, not performed: Helm waits for pods, which outlasts this request.
Whether this installs or upgrades is decided by what Helm already has.
Read the deployment to see whether it succeeded — it is done when the
status is no longer pending AND the chart version matches what was asked for.

oneOf.description: Which version, and how to fail

requestBody.description: Which version, and how to fail

post.summary: Roll a declared version out to the cluster

get.description:
Append-only: editing values writes a new version rather than changing one,
so this doubles as the record of who changed what and when.

post.summary: Add a version to a Helm deployment

get.description:
Every Helm mutation runs as a Kubernetes Job in the panel's own
namespace. This is how a caller that did not start one finds it — a page
loaded after the operation began, or after the panel's own pods were
replaced by the upgrade being watched.

Finished jobs are removed by the cluster after this lab's configured TTL,
so this is a live view rather than a history. What survives is the release
and its deployment record.

The status of one operation. `phase` is pending, running, succeeded, or
failed.

A succeeded job is not the same as a successful deploy: with
rollbackOnFailure set, a failed upgrade is undone and the job that undid
it succeeded. The completion rule is still to read the deployment and
assert both its status and its chart version.

Helm's own account of what it did, as plain text. This is where the reason
for a failed deploy is — the job's status says that it failed, not why.

A 404 with code `no_pod_yet` means the pod has not been scheduled, which
is the normal state for the first moment of every operation: retry. A 404
with `not_found` means the job is gone.

get.summary: List the Helm releases in one namespace

delete.description:
Removes the release and everything it created. Any deployment record this
lab holds is left alone — uninstalling means taking it off the cluster, not
forgetting the values that were written for it.

get.description:
The values are the ones supplied at install or upgrade, not the chart's
defaults merged with them. Re-submitting the merged set would pin every
default the chart ships with.

Newest revision first. Revisions count up and never repeat: rolling back
to revision 2 creates a new revision rather than returning to that one.

post.description:
Accepted, not performed: Helm waits for pods, which outlasts this request.
Read the release to see whether it succeeded. A rollback creates a new
revision rather than restoring the old one, so it can itself be rolled back.
post.summary: Roll a Helm release back to an earlier revision

get.description:
Across every namespace this lab has made a Helm target. A release
installed outside the panel is listed too: Helm's own storage is the
source of truth, so anything it recorded is visible here.

post.description:
The panel applies its own labels over any the request supplies: the
Pod Security enforcement level, who manages it, and the marker that
makes it a candidate for Helm. A request may not set a label under
kubernetes.io or k8s.io, since one of those decides whether a pod may
run privileged.

delete.description:
Refused for a protected namespace, and for one that still runs
workloads unless force=true. Deletion cascades to everything in the
namespace and is asynchronous: a 204 means the deletion was accepted,
and the namespace stays in the listing as Terminating until it finishes.

parameters.description: Delete even though it still runs workloads
parameters.name: force

get.description:
Most recent first, capped at 100. Events carry the reason a pod is stuck
when the pod itself only reports the symptom.

Reports a summary alongside the phase. The phase alone does not say that a
Running pod is serving nothing, or that one is being deleted.

Plain text, chunked, flushed per line. With follow=true the response stays
open and new lines arrive as they are written; closing the connection ends
it at the API server too. previous=true reads the last terminated
instance, which is where the reason for a CrashLoopBackOff lives.

parameters.description: Container; required when the pod has more than one
parameters.name: container

get.description:
Deployments, StatefulSets, and DaemonSets as one list. The question is
what is running, not which kind of controller runs it.

The workload with its pods, the services that reach them, the volume
claims they mount, and the events about any of it — in one call, because
the pieces are found by following the workload's own selector and a
client doing that would need to know how Kubernetes labels relate.

post.description:
Stamps the pod template's restartedAt annotation, the same mechanism
`kubectl rollout restart` uses, so the controller replaces its pods under
its own rollout strategy. Nothing is deleted. Deployments and
StatefulSets only.

put.description:
Sets the desired replica count through the scale subresource. Deployments
and StatefulSets only: a DaemonSet's count comes from how many nodes it
matches, so there is nothing to set.

get.description:
Capacity, what pods have reserved against it, and — when metrics-server
is installed — what is actually being used. A node whose usage is absent
reports no reading rather than zero.

Persistent volume claims and the volumes behind them. Both, because a
released volume still holding data appears in neither list alone.

Counts and totals across nodes, pods, workloads, and storage, in one call
so the dashboard neither renders nor fails in pieces.

nodes.usage is a sum over the nodes that reported a reading, so it is zero
both for an idle cluster and for one nothing measured. metricsAvailable is
what tells those apart: when it is false, treat nodes.usage as absent
rather than as a measurement of zero.

post.description:
MongoDB has no standalone create-database command: a database begins to exist
when something is put in it, so the first collection is part of the request.

oneOf.description: The database and its first collection

requestBody.description: The database and its first collection

delete.description: Removes the database and all of its data. MongoDB's own databases are refused.

post.description:
POST because the query goes in the body — it is a read, not a change. A
find and nothing else: aggregate can write through $out and $merge, and
runCommand is the whole server. Filters carrying $where, $function, or
$accumulator are refused at any depth: each runs JavaScript in the server's
engine, forcing a full collection scan and occupying a core until the
deadline. Results are capped at 200 documents and the query at 15 seconds.

get.description: MongoDB scopes a user to the database it was created in, which is where it authenticates.

parameters.description: Database the users are defined in
parameters.name: database

post.description: Roles that administer the whole server, such as root or readWriteAnyDatabase, cannot be granted here.

parameters.description: Database to create the user in
parameters.name: database

delete.description: The account this panel connects as is refused.

parameters.description: Database the user is defined in
parameters.name: database

put.description:
The whole role set, not a set of grants: MongoDB's updateUser replaces the
array outright. An empty password leaves the existing one in place.

delete.description: Removes the database and all of its data. PostgreSQL's own databases are refused.

put.description:
Only the owner. Encoding cannot be changed after creation, and a rename
would break every connection string pointing at it.

post.description:
Extensions are per database, so this installs into the named one only.
The server image ships pgvector, whose extension name is "vector".

POST because the statement goes in the body — it is a read, not a change.
Runs as the panel's own administrative account, on a connection to the named
database. What bounds it is a READ ONLY transaction that is always rolled
back, a statement timeout, and one statement per request — not a lesser
privilege, so a caller reaches whatever that account reaches. Results are
capped at 200 rows and the statement at 15 seconds.
A role that can log in needs a password. Superuser cannot be granted through this API.

delete.description: PostgreSQL's own roles and the account this panel connects as are refused.

put.description:
The whole desired state, not a set of changes: every attribute is written,
including the negative form, because ALTER ROLE leaves an unmentioned one
alone. An empty password leaves the existing one in place; a supplied one
is converted to a SCRAM verifier before it reaches the server.

get.description:
Reports who the presented bearer token belongs to. It says nothing about
what that caller may do: this API reads no permissions out of a token.

Reports whether the process is running. Checks nothing downstream, so it stays
true while a managed database is unreachable.
Returns the generated OpenAPI document describing every endpoint. Requires no authentication.
